items.title: The complement of the complement
items.prose: Let $U$ be a subspace of a finite-dimensional inner product space $V$. Prove that $(U^\perp)^\perp = U$.
items.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Let $\mathbf{u} \in U$. Each $\mathbf{w} \in U^\perp$ has $\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{w} \rangle = \overline{\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{u} \rangle} = 0$, so $U \subseteq (U^\perp)^\perp$.
Now let $\mathbf{v} \in (U^\perp)^\perp$, and write $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ with $\mathbf{u} \in U$ and $\mathbf{w} \in U^\perp$ (Axler 6.49).
$\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{u}$, and $\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{u}$ both lie in the subspace $(U^\perp)^\perp$, so $\mathbf{w}$ does too.
$\mathbf{v}$ is orthogonal to all of $U^\perp$, so $\mathbf{v} \in U$ by definition.
lines.why: Membership of $U$ is not defined by orthogonality to $U^\perp$. That is what the proof must show.

feedback.correct: Right. One inclusion is direct; the other uses the decomposition.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Prove $U \subseteq (U^\perp)^\perp$ first, then split a $\mathbf{v} \in (U^\perp)^\perp$ by Axler 6.49.

byKey.x1: You assumed the conclusion. Split $\mathbf{v}$ as $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ and show $\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{0}$.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Every $\mathbf{u} \in U$ is orthogonal to $U^\perp$, which gives one inclusion. For the other, the $U^\perp$ part of $\mathbf{v}$ lies in $U^\perp$ and its complement, so definiteness makes it $\mathbf{0}$. Finite dimension is used through Axler 6.49.

items.title: The last Lagrange polynomial
items.prose: On $\mathcal{P}_2(\mathbb{R})$ the evaluations at 0, 1 and 2 are the dual basis of $(\ell_0, \ell_1, \ell_2)$. Here $\ell_2$ is 1 at $x = 2$ and 0 at $x = 0$ and $x = 1$.
items.question: Find $\ell_2$ as a polynomial in $x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $c\,x(x - 1)$ and fix $c$ by $\ell_2(2) = 1$.

byKey.noscale: Right zeros, but $x(x - 1)$ is 2 at $x = 2$. Divide by 2.

explain.text: $\ell_2 = c\,x(x - 1)$ with $\ell_2(2) = 2c = 1$, so $c = \tfrac12$. Then $\ell_0 + \ell_1 + \ell_2 = 1$, since the sum is 1 at all three nodes. Any $p \in \mathcal{P}_2$ is $p(0)\ell_0 + p(1)\ell_1 + p(2)\ell_2$.

items.title: A dual map
items.prose: $T(x, y) = (x + 2y, 3y)$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and $\psi(x, y) = 2x - y$. The dual map gives $T'\psi = \psi \circ T$.
items.question: Find $(T'\psi)(x, y)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Substitute $T(x, y)$ into $\psi$.

byKey.trans: You multiplied by $[T]^T$ on the wrong side. The row $(2, -1)$ times $[T]$ is $(2, 1)$.
byKey.psi: You left $\psi$ unchanged. Compose it with $T$ first.

explain.text: $(\psi \circ T)(x, y) = 2(x + 2y) - 3y = 2x + y$. As rows, $(2, -1)\begin{pmatrix}1 & 2\\ 0 & 3\end{pmatrix} = (2, 1)$. In columns that is $[T]^T$ acting on $(2, -1)$, as Axler 3.114 says.

items.title: Orthonormal lines on [0, 1]
items.prose: On $\mathcal{P}_1(\mathbb{R})$ use $\langle p, q \rangle = \int_0^1 pq$. Gram-Schmidt on $(1, x)$ gives $e_1 = 1$ and $f_2 = x - \langle x, 1 \rangle 1 = x - \tfrac12$.
items.question: What is $\|f_2\|^2$, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $(x - \tfrac12)^2$ from 0 to 1.

byKey.x: That is $\|x\|^2$. Subtract the mean $\tfrac12$ first.
byKey.quarter: That is $(\tfrac12)^2$, the value at an end. Integrate the square.
byKey.root: That is $\|f_2\|$. The question asks for its square.

explain.text: $\int_0^1 (x^2 - x + \tfrac14)\,dx = \tfrac13 - \tfrac12 + \tfrac14 = \tfrac{1}{12} \approx 0.0833$. So $e_2 = \sqrt{12}(x - \tfrac12) = 2\sqrt3(x - \tfrac12)$. It is the variance of a uniform draw, which is no accident.

items.title: The best line for a parabola on [0, 1]
items.prose: With $\langle p, q \rangle = \int_0^1 pq$, find the best approximation of $x^2$ by a polynomial $a + bx$. Use the orthonormal basis $e_1 = 1$, $e_2 = 2\sqrt3(x - \tfrac12)$ of the last item.
items.question: What is $P_{\mathcal{P}_1}x^2$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\langle x^2, e_1 \rangle e_1 + \langle x^2, e_2 \rangle e_2$.

byKey.single: You added single projections onto 1 and $x$, which are not orthogonal on $[0, 1]$. Use $e_1$ and $e_2$.
byKey.const: That is only the $e_1$ part. Add $\langle x^2, e_2 \rangle e_2$.

explain.text: $\langle x^2, 1 \rangle = \tfrac13$ and $\langle x^2, e_2 \rangle = 2\sqrt3(\tfrac14 - \tfrac16) = \tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}$. So $P x^2 = \tfrac13 + \tfrac{\sqrt3}{6} \cdot 2\sqrt3(x - \tfrac12) = x - \tfrac16$. The normal equations $a + \tfrac b2 = \tfrac13$, $\tfrac a2 + \tfrac b3 = \tfrac14$ give the same $a = -\tfrac16$, $b = 1$.

items.title: Residual factors
items.prose: Write `residual_factors(R)`. The columns of $\mathbf{R}$ are daily factor returns, $n$ rows. Demean each column, then run Gram-Schmidt left to right in $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \tfrac1n\sum_k x_ky_k$. Each output column then has mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Raise `ValueError` when the demeaned columns are dependent.
items.question: Complete `residual_factors(R)`, rounded to 6 places.

tests.setup: R = np.array([[1, 2, 0], [2, 0, 1], [-1, 1, 3], [0, -2, 1], [3, 1, -1]], dtype=float); X = R - R.mean(axis=0); Q = np.array(residual_factors(R))

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests: two exact cases, unit covariance, zero means, a span check and a cash column. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

feedback.correct: Right. Demean, then Gram-Schmidt in the $\tfrac1n$ inner product.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Read the first failing row.

byKey.test-1: Demean first, and scale each column to standard deviation 1, not length 1. QR also flips signs.
byKey.test-3: Your columns have length 1. In the $\tfrac1n$ product unit norm means $\tfrac1n\sum_k q_k^2 = 1$.
byKey.test-6: A constant column, like cash, demeans to $\mathbf{0}$. Check `matrix_rank` of the demeaned matrix and raise.
byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Check the shapes in the loop.

explain.text:
The planted case is the market and factor of l13 plus constants 0.5 and 0.2, which demeaning removes. The market scales to $\mathbf{m}/\sqrt{2.5}$ and the residual $(1, 1, -1, -1)$ already has standard deviation 1. A cash column has zero variance, so it is dependent after demeaning, as in l11's trap.

```python
f -= (X[:, j] @ Q[:, i] / n) * Q[:, i]
Q[:, j] = f / np.sqrt(f @ f / n)
```

items.title: A correlation of 1.03
items.prompt: A colleague's spreadsheet shows a correlation of 1.03 between two strategies' daily returns over 20 days. (a) Prove the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality in an inner product space, with its equality case. (b) Deduce that $|\rho| \le 1$ for any two return series that are not constant. (c) The spreadsheet divides the covariance by $n - 1 = 19$ and each standard deviation by $n = 20$. Show what this does to the reported number, and find the true correlation behind 1.03. Give a reason for every line.
items.model:
**(a) Cauchy-Schwarz.** Let $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v}$ lie in an inner product space. If $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$, both sides of $|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \le \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|$ are 0. So suppose $\mathbf{v} \ne \mathbf{0}$, and set
$$c = \frac{\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2}, \qquad \mathbf{w} = \mathbf{u} - c\mathbf{v}.$$
Then $\langle \mathbf{w}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = \langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle - c\langle \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{v} \rangle = 0$, by additivity and homogeneity in the first slot. So $\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{w}$ with $c\mathbf{v} \perp \mathbf{w}$. Pythagoras gives
$$\|\mathbf{u}\|^2 = |c|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 + \|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \ge |c|^2\|\mathbf{v}\|^2 = \frac{|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle|^2}{\|\mathbf{v}\|^2},$$
since $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \ge 0$ by positivity. Multiplying by $\|\mathbf{v}\|^2$ and taking square roots gives $|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \le \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|$. Equality holds exactly when $\|\mathbf{w}\| = 0$, so when $\mathbf{u} = c\mathbf{v}$, or when $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{0}$. That is, exactly when one vector is a multiple of the other. $\blacksquare$

**(b) The bound on $\rho$.** Demean the two return series to $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{20}$. On the subspace of zero-mean vectors, $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle = \tfrac1n\sum_k x_ky_k = \mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)$ is an inner product, with norm $\|\mathbf{x}\| = \sigma_X$ (l11). If neither series is constant, both norms are positive and
$$\rho = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} = \frac{\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle}{\|\mathbf{x}\|\,\|\mathbf{y}\|}.$$
By (a), $|\rho| \le 1$, with $\rho = \pm 1$ exactly when $\mathbf{y}$ is a multiple of $\mathbf{x}$. So 1.03 cannot be a correlation.

**(c) The bug.** The spreadsheet computes
$$\frac{\tfrac{1}{n-1}\sum_k x_ky_k}{\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_k x_k^2}\,\sqrt{\tfrac1n\sum_k y_k^2}} = \frac{n}{n-1} \cdot \frac{\tfrac1n\sum_k x_ky_k}{\sigma_X\sigma_Y} = \frac{n}{n-1}\,\rho.$$
With $n = 20$ the reported number is $\tfrac{20}{19}\rho \approx 1.0526\rho$. So the true correlation behind 1.03 is $1.03 \times \tfrac{19}{20} = 0.9785$. A true 0.98 would read $0.98 \times \tfrac{20}{19} \approx 1.0316$. A seeded check agrees. Take NumPy's `default_rng(7)`, $a$ = 20 standard normals and $b = a + 0.2 \times$ 20 more. Then the true $\rho \approx 0.9749$, and the buggy ratio is $\approx 1.0262 = 0.9749 \times \tfrac{20}{19}$. The fix is to use the same divisor in the covariance and both standard deviations; it then cancels.

rubric.text: Applies Pythagoras to the orthogonal pair $c\mathbf{v}$ and $\mathbf{w}$
Drops $\|\mathbf{w}\|^2 \ge 0$ with its reason and reaches $|\langle \mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \rangle| \le \|\mathbf{u}\|\,\|\mathbf{v}\|$
States the equality case: one vector a multiple of the other
Names covariance on demeaned returns as the inner product, with the standard deviation as norm
Writes $\rho$ as $\langle \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \rangle / (\|\mathbf{x}\|\,\|\mathbf{y}\|)$, needs both norms positive, and concludes $|\rho| \le 1$
Finds the true correlation $1.03 \times \tfrac{19}{20} = 0.9785$ and names the fix

items.title: Find the flaw
items.prose: A classmate 'proves' that covariance is an inner product on all of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

rows: $\mathrm{Cov}$ is additive and homogeneous in its first argument.
So covariance is an inner product on $\mathbb{R}^n$. $\blacksquare$

items.question: Tap the line that does not follow.

feedback.correct: Right. Zero variance makes $\mathbf{x}$ constant, not zero.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test each line on a cash series that returns 0.01 every day.

byKey.r0: Line 1 is true: a mean of squares is never negative.
byKey.r1: Line 2 is true: covariance is linear in each argument.
byKey.r2: Line 3 is true: the formula is symmetric in $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{y}$.
byKey.r4: Line 5 would follow from the others. The fault is earlier.

explain.text: If every $x_k$ equals $\bar{x}$, then $\mathbf{x}$ is constant, such as cash at 0.01 a day. It need not be $\mathbf{0}$, so definiteness fails. On zero-mean vectors the step is right, since there constant means $\mathbf{0}$.

items.title: One divisor too few
items.prose: A true correlation is 0.98 over $n = 20$ days. The spreadsheet divides the covariance by $n - 1$ and both standard deviations by $n$.
items.question: What number does the spreadsheet report, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The covariance is too big by $\tfrac{n}{n-1}$; the standard deviations are right.

byKey.true: You ignored the mismatch. The covariance's divisor is smaller, so the ratio grows.
byKey.down: You scaled the wrong way: dividing by $n - 1$ makes the covariance bigger, by $\tfrac{20}{19}$.
byKey.sq: You applied the factor twice. Only the covariance uses $n - 1$.

explain.text: The covariance is $\tfrac{20}{19}$ times the $\tfrac1n$ one, and the standard deviations use $\tfrac1n$. So the ratio is $\tfrac{20}{19} \times 0.98 \approx 1.0316$. Any true correlation above $0.95$ then reads above 1.
